title: He wasn’t the king.
paragraphs:
He wasn’t the king.
He wasn’t the prophet.
But when pride got exposed, God raised up Eliakim.
The character I almost overlooked was the one God used to replace a man drunk on position.

In Isaiah 22:15–25, Shebna had the title. The wardrobe. The access. The influence. But he used his place for his own glory. He carved out significance for himself while the nation was in crisis. That is terrifying. A man can stand near holy things and still be full of himself.
Then God says, in effect: I’m removing him. I’m calling Eliakim.
And that shift is heavy.

Because Eliakim is not introduced with noise. He arrives as God’s answer to corrupted leadership. “I will clothe him with your robe… commit your authority to his hand” (Isaiah 22:21). What Shebna treated like a trophy, Eliakim received like a trust.
That’s the part that hit me.

God is not impressed with titles.
He is watching stewardship.

Shebna wanted status.
Eliakim was given responsibility.

Shebna built for self.
Eliakim became, in Scripture’s words, “a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem” (Isaiah 22:21).

And here’s what we miss: this is not just an old leadership swap in Judah. It is a mirror. Some of us keep asking God for bigger doors while carrying a Shebna spirit—self-exalting, image-driven, hungry to be seen. Meanwhile, God honors the Eliakims: steady hands, submitted hearts, shoulders strong enough to carry what belongs to Him.
Then the passage gives us that striking line: “I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David. He shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open” (Isaiah 22:22).
That language points beyond Eliakim.

In Revelation 3:7, that same authority is ultimately tied to Jesus Christ. Eliakim was a shadow. Jesus is the substance. Eliakim received delegated authority. Jesus holds absolute authority. He opens the door no man can close. He shuts what no man can force open. He is the faithful steward Shebna never was and the better King every servant needs.
So the story is not merely, “Be like Eliakim.”

The deeper message is:
Trust the greater Eliakim.
Trust Christ.

Because all of us, left to ourselves, have a little Shebna in us. We crave applause. We protect image. We confuse platform with calling. But Jesus confronts our pride, strips our false glory, and offers something better than status—grace, repentance, and a place in His house.
That’s the beauty of the Gospel.

The One with the key did not lock sinners out forever. He opened the way with His own blood. At the cross, Jesus took the ruin of proud people and made a door for the humble to come home. In Him, the self-made can be forgiven. The overlooked can be called. The unfaithful can be remade.

So don’t despise being overlooked.
God sees what pride cannot manufacture.
And when He appoints, no devil, no critic, no old title can stop it.
